parole.significato: forms the names of saturated hydrocarbons
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -ane or English -ane.

parole.significato: forms the infinitive of the second-conjugation verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese -er, from Latin -ēre. The short -ere of some Latin verbs was reinterpreted as either -er or -ir.

parole.significato: forms nouns, from adjectives, denoting states, conditions and qualities; -ness; -ity; -y; -hood
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -ia or Ancient Greek -εία (-eía).
From Old Galician-Portuguese *áaba, either from Latin ālipēs (“winged”), or from Latin alapa (“slap, smack”). Cognate with Galician aba.

From Old Galician-Portuguese abrigar, of disputed origin: most likely from Late Latin aprīcāre, from Latin aprīcārī (“to warm in the sun”), from aprīcus (“sunny”). Alternatively, and less likely, from Late Latin *abrīgāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + *brīgāre, from Frankish *birīhan (“to cover,

From Old Galician-Portuguese abrigo (“a place where one is sheltered from the elements or harm”), from abrigar, of disputed origin: possibly from Late Latin *abrīgāre (“to cover, shelter”), from a- + *brīgāre, from Frankish *biwrīhan (“to cover, protect”), from Proto-Germanic *bi- (“be-”) + *wrīhaną

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese agarimar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), perhaps from Latin *aggremiare, from Latin gremium (“lap, bosom”); alternatively from a Suevic descendant of a Proto-Germanic *ga- + *rīmą (“number, calculation”), whence Old High German girīman (“to count, to b
Borrowed from Latin agrum. Alternatively, from Old Galician-Portuguese agro. Doublet of acre.
From água + -ar. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *aquāre for Latin aquārī, or from adaquāre.
From a- + longo + -ar, or from Vulgar Latin *allongāre, from Late Latin elongāre, from Latin longus.
From alvo + -ura, or from Late Latin albūra, from Latin albus.

parole.significato: to threaten (to make a threat against someone; to use threats)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese amẽaçar, a variant of mẽaçar, either from mẽaça (“threat”) + -ar, or from a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *admināciāre (“to threaten”) < *mināciāre (“threaten”), from minācia (“threat”), from Latin mināciae. Cognate with English menace. Compare Catalan and Occitan amenaçar,
From a- + morto (“dead”) + -ecer, or from a Vulgar Latin *admortīre, *admortēscere, from Latin mortuus.
Uncertain. Either: * From antropo- + -fagia. * From antropófago + -ia. * Borrowed from French anthropophagie. * A learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀνθρωποφᾰγῐ́ᾱ (anthrōpophăgĭ́ā).

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from Vulgar Latin *appariclāre, *appariculāre, itself probably from Latin apparāre. Compare Spanish aparejar, French appareiller, Italian apparecchiare. Alternatively, it may be linked to Portuguese parelho, parelha.
Conceivably from an unattested Latin *applācāre. Alternatively, from a- + placar, from Latin plācāre. Compare with Spanish aplacar.
Borrowed from Late Latin applānāre (“to flatten”), from Latin plānus. Doublet of achanar. Alternatively, from a- + plano + -ar. Compare with Spanish aplanar.

parole.significato: to bet (to make a guess about the outcome of an event)
parole.testo: From aposta (“bet”) + -ar or from Vulgar Latin *appositāre, from Latin appositus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese aquen, from Vulgar Latin *eccum hinc, from Latin eccum + hinc, or from Vulgar Latin *eccum inde. Compare Spanish aquende, Italian quindi.

parole.significato: aura (an invisible force surrounding a living creature)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aura, from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”). Doublet of oura, which was inherited. Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English aura.

parole.significato: to monopolize; to take something for oneself without others benefiting of it
parole.testo: Uncertain, either: * From Old Galician-Portuguese *sobarcar, from Vulgar Latin *subbracchicāre, a compound of sub- + bracchium, cognate with Spanish sobarcar. * Inherited from Vulgar Latin ad se *imbracāre (“to tighten to oneself like trousers to a leg”), from a compound of in- + brāca.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Dutch bakeljauw, bakkeljauw, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Late Latin baccalaureus, baculum (“stick, staff”), referring to the way cod were split and dried on wooden sticks. Or, possibly from Basque bakailao. The Basque term may be either the source or the descendant of Dutch kabeljauw, co

parole.significato: bandana (piece of cloth worn as headgear)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Hindi बंधन (bandhan, “the act of binding, a bond”), either via English bandana or French bandana.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: paunch, fack, rumen (the first compartment of the stomach of ruminants)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Latin ventriculus, diminutive of venter; or from Vulgar Latin *pantuclus, diminutive of pantex. Cognate with Galician bandullo, Asturian bandullu, banduyu, Spanish bandujo.

parole.motivo_incerta: perhaps; alternatively; or from; either; obscure
parole.testo: Obscure. Perhaps either from Proto-Germanic *bankô (“elevation, bank”) or from *bankiz (“bench”); alternatively from the same etymon that Galician banda (“side, bank”), or from the same Celtic etymon that Irish feige.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly inherited from a Vulgar Latin *opacius, variant of opacus (“darkened, opaque”), or from Latin badius (“reddish-brown”), both terms of uncertain origin.

Borrowed from Old Occitan belleza or Italian bellezza, both from Vulgar Latin *bellitia, a noun based on Latin bellus (“pretty”). By surface analysis, belo + -eza. Compare Spanish belleza and Catalan bellesa.

parole.significato: beetle (any of numerous species of insect in the order Coleoptera)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese abesouro (“beetle”), of unknown origin. Maybe from Latin avis aurea (“golden bird”) or from Spanish abejorro, from abeja (“bee”) + -orro (“augmentative suffix”). Or, possibly imitative of the wing's sounds. Cognate with Galician abesouro (“bumblebee”).
Either from French bizarre (“strange”, “odd”, “peculiar”), or Italian bizzarro.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; either; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: pump (device for moving or compressing a liquid or gas)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Sources are divided in considering it either a derivation from etymology 1 — although neither Italian bomba or Latin bombus carry this sense — or a borrowing from French pompe, which was then reshaped by analogy.
Unknown. Perhaps related to Galician braña or from Vulgar Latin *vērānata, from Vulgar Latin *vērānum, via *verãada (compare dialectal gando). Compare also Galician branda.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese britar, from Old English brittian, or from Gothic or Suevic.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: broa (type of cornbread made in Portugal, Galicia and Brazil)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese borõa, of uncertain origin. Possibly from Gothic *𐌱𐍂𐌰𐌿𐌸 (*brauþ, “bread”), from Proto-Germanic *braudą (“cooked food, leavened bread”). Alternatively, perhaps from Paleo-Hispanic. See that entry for more. Compare Galician broa.

parole.significato: bronze (a naturally occurring or man-made alloy of copper)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French bronze, from Italian bronzo, either from Byzantine Greek βροντησίον (brontēsíon), presumably from Βρεντήσιον (Brentḗsion, “Brindisi”), known for the manufacture of bronze; or ultimately from Persian برنج (berenj, beranj, “brass”) ~ پرنگ (pereng, “copper”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese bufo, from Late Latin būfus (cognates include Spanish búho), itself either from Latin *būfō, from Faliscan *būfō, or more likely of onomatopoetic origin; cf. also Ancient Greek βοῦφος (boûphos). Compare to Latin būbō.
Unknown, perhaps from Malay buli, buli-buli (“small stoppered vial or flask of glass or porcelain”), or from Arabic بُلْبُلَة (bulbula).

From Old Galician-Portuguese buscar of unknown origin, possibly cognate with bosque, cognate with Italian buscare and Spanish buscar. Or possibly from Celtic; compare Old Irish búaid (“victory”) and Welsh budd (“gain”), all from Proto-Celtic *boudi (“gain”).
Borrowed from English bonus or Latin bonus, from Old Latin duonus, from Proto-Indo-European *dou- (“to worship”). Doublet of bom (“good”), a doublet inherited from the same Latin word.
Borrowed from Spanish cálao, either directly or via French calao, from Tagalog kalaw.
Borrowed from Provençal calhau, from Gaulish caljavo or from *caljo (“stone”).
Borrowed from Spanish candonga with the same meaning, or from Kimbundu kandonge (“weak love”), from ka- (diminutive suffix) + ndonge (“love”).

From Italian cannone (“cannon”), from Latin canna (“reed, cane”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”), from Akkadian 𒄀 (qanû, “reed”), from Sumerian 𒄀𒈾 (gi.na). Or from Spanish cañón (“cannon”) (compare cânion).
From Old Galician-Portuguese capitan, capitam, from Genoese Ligurian capitan, from Late Latin capitānus, from capitāneus, or from Latin capitālis.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; modificatore <unc> nel legame; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: snail (any animal of the class Gastropoda having a shell)
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from a derivation of Vulgar Latin *cochleār, Latin cochlea (“snail”), from Ancient Greek κοχλίας (kokhlías, “spiral, snail shell”). Compare with colher (“spoon”). Alternatively, possibly of pre-Roman substrate origin. Cognate with Galician, Asturian, and Spanish caracol, Catalan

parole.significato: rail (the metal bar that makes the track for a railroad)
parole.testo: From carro + -il, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *carrīlis, as an alteration of Late Latin currīlis, from Latin currus, with influence from carrus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: An Afro-Brazilian food made from okra, onion, shrimp, palm oil and toasted nuts.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Kimbundu kalúlu (“plant in the genus Vernonia”), or from a Paraguayan Guarani or Old Tupi ka'a ruru (literally “swollen plant”).
From Old Galician-Portuguese caseiro, from casa (“house”) + -eiro, or from Latin casārius. Compare Galician caseiro, and Spanish casero.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from the feminine of casto (“chaste”) (from Old Galician-Portuguese casto, from Latin castus) or from Gothic *𐌺𐌰𐍃𐍄𐌰𐌽 (*kastan) or *𐌺𐌰𐍃𐍄𐍃 (*kasts), from Proto-Germanic *kastōną (“to throw, cast”), *kastuz.

parole.significato: funk (foul or unpleasant smell, especially body odour)
parole.testo: Unknown. Borrowed from either Old Tupi katinga or Kimbundu katinga.

parole.significato: fence (thin barrier that separates two pieces of land)
parole.testo: Deverbal from cercar (“surround”), or from Old Galician-Portuguese cerca (“surround”), from a Vulgar Latin *circa (compare Spanish cerca, northern Italian cerca, French cerce), from the feminine of Latin circus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from French chape, chappe, from Latin cappa (“cape”), or from a root *klapa.
Unknown. Possibly from a pre-Roman Paleo-Hispanic substrate, or from North Germanic/Scandinavian flark. Compare Spanish charco, from which it could have been borrowed.

parole.significato: arrival (act of arriving or something that has arrived)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese chegada, from chegar (“arrive”), from Latin plicāre (“fold up, arrive”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”); alternatively, chegar + -ada.

Probably either borrowed from Italian cicoria or perhaps from a Mozarabic form (cf. Spanish achicoria), from Vulgar Latin and Late Latin cichoria, from the plural of Latin cichorium, from Ancient Greek κιχόριον (kikhórion).
From Spanish chubasco, from Portuguese chuva + Spanish suffix -sco. Or from Galician chuvasco. Compare Italian piovasco.
From Old Galician-Portuguese cobertor, from Latin coopertōrium, or from cobrir, coberto + -(t)or. Cf. also the rare or archaic cobertouro, and Galician cobertoiro.
From comprar + -dor, or from Late Latin compārātōrem, from Latin compārō.
From Latin cōmoedia, from Ancient Greek κωμῳδία (kōmōidía), from κῶμος (kômos, “revel, caurousing”) + either ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) or ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer, bard”), both from ἀείδω (aeídō, “to sing”).

parole.significato: courage; boldness; guts (the quality of not being scared easily)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge or Old French corage, from Latin cor (“heart”).

parole.significato: mail (regular delivery of letters and small parcels)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan corrieu (“messenger”) (Catalan correu), from Old French corlieu, or from Spanish correo.
From Late Latin corrōsiō, corrōsiōnem, from corrōsus, perfect passive participle of corrōdō. Alternatively, from French corrosion.

parole.significato: pirate; corsair (one who plunders at sea)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian corsaro, from Medieval Latin cursārius. Alternatively, reformed from earlier cossário and cossairo as corso + -ário.

Ultimately from Latin cubitum (“elbow”) through Old Galician-Portuguese *covetelo, either from Latin cubitālis (via Mozarabic qubtal) or alternatively from Latin cubitellum. Cognate with Galician cotobelo. Cf. also the related coto and côvado.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cova, from Vulgar Latin *cova, from covus, alternative form of Latin cavus (or from a variant of Late Latin cava, from cavum, cavus), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱówHwos (“cavity”). Compare Spanish cueva.
From cravo + -ar, from Old Galician-Portuguese cravo (“nail”), from Latin clāvus (“nail”), or from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus.

From Old Galician-Portuguese cambio, either directly from Late Latin cambium (“change”) or deverbal of cambiar (cf. Portuguese escambo), from Latin cambiāre (“to change”), from a Celtic language, from Proto-Celtic *kamb- (“crooked; bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ḱamb-, *(s)kamb- (“bent”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese dado, itself from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, of uncertain origin; possibly from Classical Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”), or from Latin datum. Compare Spanish dado, Catalan dau, Italian dado, French dé.
From Old Galician-Portuguese derramar, in turn from ramo, or from a Vulgar Latin *dīrāmāre or *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Italian diramare, Romanian dărâma.

From Old Galician-Portuguese derrobar, from Vulgar Latin *dērūpāre, from Latin rūpēs (“cliff”). Alternatively from derribar, from de- + riba + -ar, from Latin rīpa. Compare Galician derrubar, cf. also Italian dirupare.

From Old Galician-Portuguese descalço, from Vulgar Latin *discalceus, itself either from a shortening of discalceātus, from Late Latin discalceō, or from Latin dis- + calceus. Cognate with Galician and Spanish descalzo, Catalan descalç, Occitan descauç, French déchaux, Italian scalzo and Romanian de

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese dourado (past participle of dourar), or from Latin dēaurātus, or from dē- + aurātus (“golden”), from aurum (“gold”). Compare Galician dourado, Spanish dorado, French doré.

parole.significato: gift (something given without charge as a gesture of good will)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese dadiva, from Latin datīva, plural of datīvum. The shift in stress is possibly due to the influence of dēbita (“debt”), from the tendency of learned words having stress on their first syllable, or from the reinterpretation of the word as dado (“given”) with a suffix.

parole.significato: to adorn; to decorate (to add ornaments and decorations)
parole.testo: From earlier afeitar, from Latin affectāre. Doublet of afetar and afectar. Alternatively, from Latin īnfectus (“dyed”). If so, it is a doublet of infectar instead.

parole.significato: engineer (person qualified or professionally engaged in engineering)
parole.testo: Calque of Medieval Latin ingeniārius (“one who makes or uses an engine”), composed of inherited engenho + -eiro, from Latin ingenium (“an engine”). Alternatively a calque of French ingénieur composed in the same fashion. Compare also Spanish ingeniero.
From gola, or from an Old Galician-Portuguese engolir, from a Vulgar Latin *ingullīre, from Latin gula.

parole.significato: to evil-eye (to cast an evil eye)
parole.testo: Possibly from Gothic 𐌹𐌽𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍄𐌰𐌽 (inweitan) or from Vulgar Latin *inīquitiāre.
From en- + teso + -ar; or from Vulgar Latin *intēnsāre, from Latin intēnsus, whence Portuguese intenso. Compare Spanish entesar, Occitan entesar, Old French entaisier. See also teso.
From Old Galician-Portuguese erro, from earlier error, borrowed from Latin errōrem; alternatively, a deverbal from errar (compare Spanish yerro).

From Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐌲𐌺𐌾𐌰 (*skagkja), or from Old French eschanson, from Frankish *skankjo, both from Proto-Germanic *skankijô (“server or pourer of drinks”), from *skankijaną (“to pour in, serve drinks”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)keng- (“to limp, be crooked, slant”).

From Old French escarlate (“scarlet cloth”), from Medieval Latin scarlatum (“scarlet cloth”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Persian سقرلاط (saqerlât, “a warm woollen cloth”), a variant of سقلاط (seqellât, “scarlet cloth”), from Byzantine Greek σιγιλλᾶτος (sigillâtos), ultimately from Latin

parole.significato: to rub (move one object while maintaining contact with another object over some area)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfricāre, from Latin ex- + fricō (“to rub”), or from an alteration of effricāre.

parole.significato: to spectate, especially in the context of a video game
parole.testo: Likely from English spectate. Alternatively, learned borrowing from Latin spectāre.

parole.significato: skewer; spit (long pin used to secure food during cooking)
parole.testo: Probably from Gothic *𐍃𐍀𐌹𐍄𐌿𐍃 (*spitus), from Proto-Germanic *spitō (“rod”); alternatively from a Gothic or Suevic form derived from Proto-Germanic *speutą (“spear”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish espeto. Compare also English spit and Swedish spett.
From espinha + -al, or from Late Latin spīnālis, from Latin spīna.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese esteo, either: * borrowed from Old French estai, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stagą * inherited from Latin stilus. In this case, it is a doublet of estilo and style. Cognate with Galician esteo.

parole.significato: to hinder; to hamper (to delay or impede movement or progress)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese estorvar, either from Latin exturbāre or from Old Galician-Portuguese destorvar, from disturbāre. Compare Spanish estorbar, Catalan and Occitan destorbar, Old French destorber.

parole.significato: to think that something is unusual or weird, to be surprised
parole.testo: From estranho (“strange/stranger”) + -ar. Alternatively, inherited from Late Latin extrāneāre, from Latin extrāneus. Compare Spanish extrañar, Galician and Asturian estrañar, Catalan estranyar.
Borrowed from Late Latin extēnsīvus, from Latin extēnsus. Alternatively, borrowed from French extensif, of the same Latin origins.

From falha, itself from a Vulgar Latin falla or falia (possibly partly through the intermediate or influence of Old French faille or Old Occitan), or from Old Galician-Portuguese fallar, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.
From Old Galician-Portuguese falsar (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), either from Late Latin falsāre or a new verb formed on falso (“false”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese faisca, feisca (attested in Medieval Latin as falisca), of uncertain origin. Possibly from Proto-Germanic *falwiskǭ (“spark, ash over burning ambers”), from Proto-Germanic *falwaz (“fallow”) from Proto-Indo-European *polʷos, or from Vulgar Latin *favillesca, from favilla

parole.significato: to horseshoe (to apply horseshoes to a horse or other hooved animal)
parole.testo: From ferro (“iron”) + -ar, or from a Late Latin ferrāre, from Latin ferrum (“iron”). Compare Spanish herrar, Catalan ferrar, French ferrer, Italian ferrare.

parole.significato: snout (long, projecting nose, mouth, and jaw of a beast)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin faucinus, a diminutive of Latin faucēs (“throat, gullet”). Alternatively, influenced by Spanish hocicar (“to root with the nose”), ultimately from Latin fodere (“to dig”). Cognate with Galician fociño. Compare also Spanish hocico and Asturian focicu.
Maybe from Spanish cohete (influenced by fogo (“fire”)), from Catalan coet, from Latin coda; or from fogo + -ete.
Borrowed from French fraise or from Vulgar Latin *frēsāre, from frēsum, past participle of Latin frendēre (“to grind”). See also Spanish fresa.

parole.significato: throat (posterior region of the oral cavity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese garganta; from a substrate language *gʷr̥h₃gn̥t- (“throat”), cognate with Proto-Celtic *brāgants (“neck, throat”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₃- (“to swallow”). Alternatively, onomatopoeic.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; or possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese gavian, of uncertain origin. Possible etymologies include: * From Latin gāvia (“kind of bird; seagull”), with the suffix -ão, or possibly through a Vulgar Latin *gavianus (compare Italian gabbiano); compare gaivota from the same etymon; * From Gothic *𐌲𐌰𐌱𐌹𐌻𐌰 (*gabila, “s
Uncertain. Maybe from Spanish jineta or from Arabic.
From Latin grenniō, or from a Celtic language via Spanish greña (shag, mop).
From Old Galician-Portuguese grito, from gritar, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre, either from Latin quirītō or Frankish *krītan.
From Old Galician-Portuguese gru m, from Latin gruem f or m (“crane”) or possibly through a Vulgar Latin *gruum m, from Proto-Indo-European *gr̥h₂ú-, from *gerh₂- (“to cry hoarsely”).
Borrowed from either French guindeau or Old French guindas, which are from Provençal guindatz and ultimately from Old Norse vindáss.
Perhaps onomatopoeic or from a Germanic language: compare English whisk, from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz (“bundle”). Cognate with Galician guizo and Spanish guizque (“sting”).

Unknown. May be related to geringonça (“argot”) and Spanish jerga (“slang, jargon”). Alternatively, perhaps from Proto-Celtic *garyos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵeh₂r-, or a derivation from germania.

From Old Galician-Portuguese, from justo + -eza, or possibly from Latin iūstitia. Compare Spanish justeza, Galician and Asturian xusteza, Catalan and Occitan justesa, French justesse, Italian giustezza, Friulian justece. See also justiça, possibly a doublet.

Either borrowed from Spanish ladino or re-Latinized after Latin latinus. The inherited form from Vulgar Latin is Portuguese ladinho. Doublet of latino, which was a later borrowing. The sense of "sly" developed from a sense of "learned", in reference to learned people who knew Classical Latin.

parole.significato: a vat in which olives and grapes are pressed
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from lago or from a Vulgar Latin *lacālis, from Latin lacus.

Borrowed from French lampion, from Italian lampione (from lampa + -one). The origins of the "supporter of S.L. Benfica" sense are unclear. The two most likely theories being that either a reference to Lampião, a famous Brazilian bandit; or a riff on S.L.B.'s home turf of Luz (literally, “light”).
From Latin latus (“wide, extensive”); or from Italian latta (“tin can”).
From lavar + -dura, or from a Vulgar Latin root *lavatūra, from Latin lavō.
From lavandeiro (“launderer”), from Late Latin lavandārius, or from French lavandière. Compare also Spanish lavandera, Asturian llavandera.
From Suevic *lāwerka, or from Gothic *𐌻𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌴𐍂𐌺𐍉 (*laiwērkō), from Proto-Germanic *laiwazikǭ.

Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *listiz; compare Old High German and Old Norse lista, English list, Italian lesto and Spanish listo. Alternatively, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *lextus or *lestus, reduced from *lexitus, as an alteration of Latin lēctus (“chosen; read”), participle of legō.

parole.significato: to clean (to remove dirt from a place or object)
parole.testo: From limpo (“clean”) + -ar, or from Old Galician-Portuguese, from Late Latin limpidāre, from Latin limpidus (“clear; limpid”). Compare Spanish limpiar.

A Germanic borrowing, from Proto-West Germanic *hlut, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą (“lot, share”), either through Suevic or through Old French lot. The Germanic source could have instead been Gothic 𐌷𐌻𐌰𐌿𐍄𐍃 (hlauts).
Borrowed from French macle, either from Latin macula (from Italic) or from Medieval Latin mascula (from Germanic); see French and English macle for more.

parole.significato: mottled (coloured in patches), spotted, speckled, piebald
parole.testo: From malha, or from Old Galician-Portuguese mallado, from an Iberian Vulgar Latin *mac(u)lātus, from Latin macula. Compare Spanish majada. The origin of the "supporter of queen Maria II, liberal" sense is unclear. A popular theory postulates it was coined by partisans of Dom Miguel (Maria II's rival
From earlier mangal, from mango (“flail shaft”), from Vulgar Latin *manicus (“handle”), from Latin manus (“hand”). Alternatively, from Latin manuālis.

From Old Galician-Portuguese martelo, from Late Latin martellus, itself a diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, or alternatively based on malleus. Compare Galician martelo, Spanish martillo, Catalan martell, and Italian martello.
Borrowed from Nheengatu and Old Tupi matamatá.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Likely from a Bantu language, either from Kimbundu misanga, plural of musanga, or from Nyungwe maussanga, plural of usanga.

parole.significato: to mix (stir two or more substances together)
parole.testo: From mistura (“mixture”) + -ar (forms infinitives), from Latin mīxtura, feminine participle of misceō (“to mix”), from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵ-, *meiḱ- (“to mix”). Alternatively from Old Galician-Portuguese mesturar, from a Late Latin mixturāre, from Latin mīxtura. Compare Italian misturare, archa
Said to be either from Kongo makooto or Old Tupi mbokotóg.

parole.significato: miller (person who operates or runs a mill)
parole.testo: From Latin molinārius (through an Old Galician-Portuguese form molneiro, following syncopation), or possibly molārius. Compare Spanish molero.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Either from Vulgar Latin *moranicum, from Latin morum (“mulberry”) or from amora (“bramble; blackberry”) + -ango. Compare Galician amorodo, amorogo (“strawberry”). Displaced Latin fragum, which, if it followed the same development in other romance language, probably would have yielded eit

parole.significato: wall (structure built for defence surrounding or separating an area)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian muraglia (“wall”), muro (“wall”) + -aglia, or from Late Latin muralia, from Latin mūrus.
Learned borrowing from Latin mīmicus. Noun 2 sense 1 is a semantic loan from English mimic.

Learned borrowing from Latin nāvigātōrem, from nāvigō (“to sail, to navigate”). By surface analysis, navegar + -dor. Noun 2 sense 1 and noun 2 sense 2 are semantic loans from English navigator, likely influenced by DOS Navigator and Netscape Navigator.
From Old Portuguese ola + -eiro, or possibly from or Late Latin ollārius, from Latin ōlla.
Merger of Old Tupi urukuri and ûakury.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from para- + fuso, from Medieval Latin *pare fusu or from Spanish parahúso.

parole.significato: small meal in the morning of a working day, before or after the breakfast, traditionally accompanied by wine or aguarde…
parole.testo: With the first meaning, attested since 1807. From Latin parvus (“small; unimportant”), or from its diminutive parvulus; from Proto-Indo-European *ph₁w- (“few, small”).
From French passerelle, either directly or via Italian passerella. Cognate with Spanish pasarela.

parole.significato: jug with a capacity of approximately a litre
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese pichel (13th century, Cantigas de Santa Maria), from Old French pichier (“small jug”), from Late Latin pīcārium, alteration of bīcārium, itself possibly from bacarium, bacar or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos). Compare English pitcher; more at beaker.
From piolho + -oso, or from Vulgar Latin peduclōsus, from Latin peduculōsus, variant of pēdīculōsus analogous to peduculus.
Uncertain. Either from Vulgar Latin *planea, from Latin plāna; from plana, feminine of plano; or a back-formation from aplainar.

parole.significato: pigsty (shelter or enclosure where pigs are kept)
parole.testo: From an Old Galician-Portuguese *porcilga, related to porco (“pig”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin *porcicula (with metathesis and later contraction), itself possibly from a crossing of Late Latin porcīle, from Latin porcus, and *cōrtīcula, diminutive of Latin cōrtem (“farmyard or enclosure”), or
From portar + -dor, or from Late Latin portātōrem, from Latin portō.

parole.significato: propane (aliphatic hydrocarbon, a constituent of natural gas)
parole.testo: Borrowed from English propane or French propane.
From Old Galician-Portuguese prova, either regressively derived from the verb provar or from Late Latin proba (“proof”), from Latin probō (“to approve; to prove”), from probus (“good”).

parole.significato: courtyard (an area, open to the sky, partially or wholly surrounded by walls or buildings)
parole.testo: From Old Occitan patu or pati, from Latin pactum (“pact, agreement”) or from Latin pateō (“to lie open”).
From queijo + -eiro, or from Late Latin cāseārius, from Latin cāseus. Compare Spanish quesero.

parole.significato: a kind of French toast, prepared as dessert during Christmas period
parole.testo: Borrowed from Spanish rebanada (“a slice (of bread)”), from rebanar (“to slice”), from Latin rapināre; or from rábano (“turnip, horseradish”) + -ada.
Uncertain. Likely from raio (“beam”) + -a (forms feminine equivalents), or from an equivalent Vulgar Latin *radia, ultimately from Latin radius. Cognates include Galician raia and Spanish raya.
Borrowed from English reactor or from French réacteur.
From Old Galician-Portuguese renda, probably from Old Catalan or Old Occitan renda, either way from Early Medieval Latin rendita. Compare Galician renda, Spanish renta.
From Old Galician-Portuguese [Term?], from a Vulgar Latin root *remussicāre, itself an alteration of *remussitāre, from Latin mussitāre, or from mussō. Compare Spanish remusgar.
Borrowed from French rime, from Old French rime; or from Medieval Latin rhythmus.
From Old Galician-Portuguese saya, from Vulgar Latin *săgĭa, from Latin sagum, from Gaulish *sagos or from Ancient Greek σάγος (ságos) (cloak); cognate with Galician saia and archaic Spanish saya.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A Cape Verdean who is not from Santiago, especially one from the Barlavento islands, Fogo, or Brava.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Kabuverdianu sanpadjudu, of uncertain origin. * Possibly from são para ajuda (“they're for help”). According to this account, the term referred to people from the other islands who were brought to Santiago to assist with agricultural work under the colonial government. * Alternatively,
From Old Galician-Portuguese sanguento, sangoento, from Latin sanguinentus, from sanguis (“blood”); alternatively, sangue + -ento.
From Old Galician-Portuguese, a semi-learned borrowing from Latin sānitātem, or from são + -idade. Doublet of sanita.
Borrowed from Old Tupi sarará. Etymology 1, noun 2 sense 1 was first attested in 1900 and is likely a semantic loan from Nheengatu sarará.

From Paleo-Hispanic (compare Basque sasi, earlier çarzi). Alternatively, from Arabic شَرَا (šarā, “plant with thorns”), from سَارَاسَا (sārāsā, “to be evil, vicious”). Cognate with Asturian, Spanish, and Ladino zarza.

From Old Galician-Portuguese seita, from Latin secta (“sect”), probably from sectus (“cut off”), perfect passive participle of secō (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”), or alternatively from sequor.
From solto + -ar or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *soltāre (a root) < *solutāre, as a frequentative of Latin solvere.

From soluço, or from Old Galician-Portuguese solluçar, from Vulgar Latin *suggluttiāre, from singultō (“to gasp, to hiccup”) (with the prefix sub- and altered by influence from gluttiō (“to swallow”)), from Latin singultus. Compare Galician saloucar, Spanish sollozar, Romanian sughița, also Italian

From Old Galician-Portuguese son (probably influenced by or possibly borrowed from Old Occitan son), from Latin sonus. Alternatively, regressively derived from the verb soar. Compare Galician and Spanish son.
From Latin sonitum, either as a semi-learned borrowing or via Spanish sonido.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese soprar, *soplar, probably a semi-learned term derived from Latin sufflāre (“to blow, to puff up, to inflate”). Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *supplāre, *sopplāre. Cognate with Galician soprar, Spanish soplar and Venetan supiar.

parole.significato: to bury, to cover in dirt, snow or rubble
parole.testo: From so- (“under”) + terra (“earth”) + -ar or possibly from Late Latin subterrāre, from Latin sub- + terra.

Borrowed from Spanish zozobrar or Old Spanish sozobrar, from Old Catalan sotsobrar, from sotsobre < sots + sobre, or from a Vulgar Latin *subsuperāre (“turn upside down”), from sub (“under”) + super (“over”).

parole.significato: to emerge from the earth like a spring
parole.testo: From or related to surto, from Vulgar Latin *sūrctus, a corruption of Latin surrēctus, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *sūrctīre, derived from this root. Related to surgir. Alternatively from or influenced by Old French sourdre.

parole.significato: sound, healthy (enjoying health and vigour of body, mind, or spirit)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese são, from Latin sānus, either from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂-no- (“to satisfy”) or possibly from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”). Doublet of sano. Cognate with Galician san and Spanish sano.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from Breton tann or from Low German tanu.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese tecer, from Latin texere, from Proto-Italic *teksō, either from Proto-Indo-European *tḗtḱ-ti or from *teḱ-se-ti, both from *teḱ- (“to beget, produce”). Compare Galician tecer, Spanish tejer.
Borrowed from English telephone or French téléphone. By surface analysis, tele- + -fone.

parole.significato: telephone (a telecommunication device used for two-way talking with another person)
parole.testo: Borrowed either from Spanish teléfono (“telephone”) or Venetan tełefono (“telephone”).

From Old Galician-Portuguese teta, possibly from Frankish *titta, from Proto-Germanic *titt- (“teat; nipple; breast”), from Proto-Indo-European *tata- (“father; parent; nipple”), or less likely Ancient Greek τίτθη (títthē). Alternatively, an expressive formation. Compare Spanish teta, French tette,
Either deverbal from tirotear or from Spanish tiroteo; otherwise directly from tiro. Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

parole.significato: auger (tool for boring holes in wood)
parole.testo: From Old Galician-Portuguese traado (13th century), from Late Latin taratrum (“auger”), attested by Isidore of Seville. Either from Paleo-Hispanic or from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *taratrom, from Proto-Indo-European *térh₁-tro-. Alternatively from Ancient Greek τέρετρον (téretron, “borer, gimlet”)

parole.significato: to inhale smoke from a cigarette
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *tragāre, possibly from Doric Greek τράγω (trágō), in which case cognate with Attic Greek τρώγω (trṓgō, “to eat, to swallow”). Alternatively, Coromines suggests an origin ultimately in dracō (“dragon”), via an attested tracō (“underground cavern”), in the sense of "that which swall

From Old Galician-Portuguese trõo, from trõar, or alternatively from Latin tonus (“thunderclap; sound, tone”), probably through a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin form *tronus, influenced by *tronitus < tonitrus. Compare Galician trono, Spanish trueno, Catalan tro, Occitan tron. See also tom, a possible d

parole.significato: any automobile used to transport people or goods
parole.testo: Borrowed from French voiture (“car, wagon”), from Latin vectūra (“transportation, fare, wagon”), feminine of vectūrus, the future active participle of vehō (“to carry, to bear”, root also of veículo (“vehicle”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to bring, to transport”), thus distantly r
From Vulgar Latin *virāre, either from Latin gȳrāre (making it a doublet of girar) or from Latin vibrāre (making it a doublet of vibrar). Compare Catalan virar, French virer and Italian virare.

parole.significato: to sail, to row (of a person or people: to move over a body of water by means of sails or oars)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Catalan vogar, itself possibly from Latin vocāre (“call”), or alternatively related to French vogue, voguer, and of Germanic origin. Compare also Spanish bogar, Italian vogare.
Either borrowed from English windsurf, or a partial calque of English windsurfing, from English wind + surfe.

parole.significato: to devotedly take care of something
parole.testo: From zelo (“zeal”) + -ar, or from Late Latin zēlāre, from Ancient Greek ζήλος (zḗlos, “zeal; jealousy”).
